title: Thyme infusion for gut wind and cramps
subtitle: A carminative cup for digestive spasm
excerpt: A hot infusion of fresh or dried thyme for gut wind, digestive cramps, and a tense or unsettled stomach. One teaspoon of dried thyme per 200 ml, steeped covered for eight minutes, makes a pale golden, warmly aromatic cup. A different preparation from thyme cough syrup: this is the digestive use.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), thyme entry: notes carminative and antispasmodic action for the digestive tract alongside the more well-known respiratory uses. Culpeper, The English Physician (1652), thyme entry: records use for colic and wind. BHP (1983) thyme monograph: dosing reference. EMA HMPC monograph on Thymi herba (2013): safety note on pregnancy at therapeutic doses.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dried thyme stores 12 months in a sealed jar or tin away from light. Fresh thyme can be used as an alternative; use 2 teaspoons of fresh sprigs in place of 1 teaspoon dried. Prepare each cup fresh.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Prepare fresh for each dose. Do not store the brewed infusion.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preparation made by pouring just-boiled water over leaves or flowers and steeping them covered, so the volatile oils stay in the cup rather than escaping with the steam.
A herb that relaxes the smooth muscle of the digestive tract and helps to release trapped gas, traditionally easing bloating and cramping.

content.text: Thyme infusion is a hot, pale golden cup of fresh or dried thyme steeped in just-boiled water. While thyme is better known as the base for a cough remedy, this is the digestive preparation: western herbalists have long used it as a

for gut wind, cramping after a meal, and a tense or spasmodic gut. One teaspoon of dried thyme per 200 ml, steeped covered for eight minutes, makes one cup; dried thyme keeps well for a year in a sealed jar.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body:
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Pregnancy: culinary use of thyme in cooking is well tolerated. A therapeutic-strength tea taken daily is a different matter. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using this remedy in pregnancy.

No significant drug interactions are documented for thyme leaf infusion at standard culinary or medicinal-tea doses.

Paediatric use is not adult-divided-by-half. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine, or a paediatric doctor, before using any herbal preparation in children under twelve.

items.prepNote: dried leaf and stem, or 2 tsp fresh sprigs

content.text: Put 1 teaspoon of dried thyme (or 2 teaspoons of fresh sprigs) into a teapot or covered cup.
Pour over 200 ml of just-boiled water and put the lid on at once.
Steep covered for 8 minutes. The water turns a warm golden-green and smells clearly of thyme.
Strain through a sieve and drink warm.
One cup (200 ml) up to three times a day, taken after meals or when symptoms arise. For an acute episode of wind or cramping: up to one week. If symptoms persist beyond a week, see your doctor.

Prepare each cup fresh. Dried thyme stores in a sealed tin or jar, away from light and heat, for up to 12 months. Fresh thyme keeps in the fridge for up to a week, or dried and stored for the full year.
When not to use this remedy
See a doctor for severe cramping, cramp that comes with fever. Vomiting, or blood in the stool, or any colic that does not improve within a day or two of self-care.
Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using this remedy in pregnancy. Do not use in children under twelve without specialist paediatric guidance.

items.symptom: Cup tastes strongly medicinal or unpleasant
items.cause: Steeped too long, or used too much herb
items.fix: Keep to 8 minutes and 1 teaspoon dried. Thyme is aromatic enough that over-steeping quickly becomes overpowering.

items.cause: Dried thyme is old or poorly stored
items.fix: Replace the dried herb. It should smell clearly of thyme when rubbed between the fingers.
